Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)

- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace

Muffet is a fast website link checker which scrapes and inspects all pages in a website recursively.

## Features

- Massive speed
- High compatibility with web browsers
- Different tag support (`a`, `img`, `link`, `script`, etc)
- Multiple output formats (text, JSON, and JUnit XML)

go install github.com/raviqqe/muffet/v2@latest

docker pull raviqqe/muffet

muffet https://example.com

input.command: # Interesting - robots.txt is checked but when pages return 200, they're all still checked # The key distinction is: links are checked (fetched) but disallowed pages are not SCRAPED # So scraping means: following the links on that page # But the links themselves are still fetched for status codes # Let me test with the earlier server that had disallowed links # and make disallowed page have its own links that wouldn't be followed cat > /tmp/check_robots2.py << 'EOF' import http.server html = b''' Allowed Disallowed ''' allowed_page = b''' From allowed ''' disallowed_page = b''' From disallowed ''' robots_txt = b'''User-agent: * Disallow: /disallowed-page ''' class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler): def log_message(self, format, *args): pass def do_GET(self): if self.path == '/': self.send_response(200) self.send_header('Content-Type', 'text/html') self.end_headers() self.wfile.write(html) elif self.path == '/allowed-page': self.send_response(200) self.send_header('Content-Type', 'text/html') self.end_headers() self.wfile.write(allowed_page) elif self.path == '/disallowed-page': self.send_response(200) self.send_header('Content-Type', 'text/html') self.end_headers() self.wfile.write(disallowed_page) elif self.path == '/robots.txt': self.send_response(200) self.send_header('Content-Type', 'text/plain') self.end_headers() self.wfile.write(robots_txt) else: self.send_response(200) self.end_headers() server = http.server.HTTPServer(('localhost', 8783), Handler) print('started', flush=True) server.serve_forever() EOF python3 /tmp/check_robots2.py & sleep 1 echo "Without robots.txt:" ./executable http://localhost:8783 -v 2>&1 echo "" echo "With robots.txt:" ./executable http://localhost:8783 --follow-robots-txt -v 2>&1

# Perfect! With --follow-sitemap-xml:
# Pages in sitemap are scraped
# Pages NOT in sitemap are checked (for status) but not scraped
# This is the same behavior as --follow-robots-txt

# Now I have enough understanding. Let me check what User-Agent the tool sends
cat > /tmp/check_ua.py << 'EOF'
import http.server

class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def log_message(self, format, *args):
        pass
    def do_GET(self):
        ua = self.headers.get('User-Agent', 'NOT SET')
        print(f'User-Agent: {ua}', flush=True)
        if self.path == '/':
            self.send_response(200)
            self.send_header('Content-Type', 'text/html')
            self.end_headers()
            self.wfile.write(b'<html><body></body></html>')
        elif self.path == '/robots.txt':
            self.send_response(200)
            self.send_header('Content-Type', 'text/plain')
            self.end_headers()
            self.wfile.write(b'User-agent: *\nDisallow:\n')
        else:
            self.send_response(200)
            self.end_headers()

server = http.server.HTTPServer(('localhost', 8787), Handler)
print('started', flush=True)
server.serve_forever()
EOF
python3 /tmp/check_ua.py &
sleep 1
./executable http://localhost:8787 -v 2>&1

Client.Timeout - when the request/response times out # We saw "timeout" for a response timeout # "dialing to the given TCP address timed out" would be for connection establishment timeout # But with Go's net/http, the Timeout applies to the whole request including connection # Let me just make sure I match the error format correctly # Also important - let me verify the URL normalisation for sub-page results cat > /tmp/check_url_norm.py << 'EOF' import http.server html = b'Page' html2 = b'Home' class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler): def log_message(self, format, *args): pass def do_GET(self): if self.path == '/': self.send_response(200) self.send_header('Content-Type', 'text/html') self.end_headers() self.wfile.write(html) elif self.path == '/page': self.send_response(200) self.send_header('Content-Type', 'text/html') self.end_headers() self.wfile.write(html2) else: self.send_response(404) self.end_headers() server = http.server.HTTPServer(('localhost', 8809), Handler) print('started', flush=True) server.serve_forever() EOF python3 /tmp/check_url_norm.py & sleep 1 echo "URL normalization:" /workspace/executable http://localhost:8809 -v 2>&1 echo "---" /workspace/muffet_test http://localhost:8809 -v 2>&1

input.command: # I see! /sub is being fetched 3 times # That's wrong. Let me investigate # The issue is: # 1. Root page http://localhost:8810 -> fetches http://localhost:8810 -> body with link to /sub # - The page URL is stored as "http://localhost:8810" # 2. Link /sub -> resolved to http://localhost:8810/sub # - Added to visited: http://localhost:8810/sub # - Queued for scraping # 3. Also, http://localhost:8810/ gets added to visited too somehow? # Actually no... # # Wait - in processPage, I call extractLinks which resolves to http://localhost:8810/sub # Then checkLink gets called for http://localhost:8810/sub # That's one fetch # Then in the success case, maybeQueueScrape is called for http://localhost:8810/sub # That's TWO more fetches (one in scrape, and checkLink also fetches) # # Oh! The problem is: checkLink fetches the URL, AND scrape also fetches it # That's double-fetching # Also the root page is being shown as http://localhost:8810 (without /) but actual URL is / # I need to fix: # 1. Don't fetch pages twice - when we check a link, we should cache the result # 2. The root URL should be normalized # Let me look at this more carefully # In the original: each URL is fetched only ONCE # The check and scrape use the same fetch # The correct approach: # 1. Fetch the URL for link checking # 2. If it's HTML, also scrape it # Both happen in the same fetch # Let me restructure the crawler: # - Process pages: fetch once, check status + extract links + scrape # - Link checking is just status checking (not body reading for non-HTML) # Actually looking at this again: # - checkLink: fetches to check status, returns result # - scrape: fetches to extract links from HTML # # For HTML pages: they get fetched ONCE in checkLink, and the body is available # Then they ALSO get fetched in scrape # That's the double-fetch issue # # The correct approach: when checking a link, if it's HTML, cache the body # and use it in scrape # But that's complex. A simpler approach: # - Don't call checkLink separately for pages that will be scraped # - Instead, scrape the page and report the status from the scrape # Wait, but some links might appear multiple times across different pages # The original seems to only fetch each URL once # Let me re-examine the original behavior cat > /tmp/check_fetch.py << 'EOF' import http.server count = {} class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler): def log_message(self, format, *args): pass def do_GET(self): count[self.path] = count.get(self.path, 0) + 1 print(f'GET {self.path} (count: {count[self.path]})', flush=True) self.send_response(200) self.send_header('Content-Type', 'text/html') self.end_headers() if self.path == '/': self.wfile.write(b'p1p2') elif self.path == '/page1': self.wfile.write(b'shared') elif self.path == '/page2': self.wfile.write(b'shared') else: self.wfile.write(b'') server = http.server.HTTPServer(('localhost', 8811), Handler) print('started', flush=True) server.serve_forever() EOF python3 /tmp/check_fetch.py & sleep 1 /workspace/executable http://localhost:8811 -v 2>&1 echo "---" echo "Fetch counts above"

# Perfect! Each URL fetched exactly once in the original
# Now let me redesign my crawler

# The key insight: 
# There's a global "URL result cache" - each URL is checked ONCE
# When a page processes its links, it:
# 1. Checks if URL already has a result (cached)
# 2. If not, fetches the URL and caches the result
# 3. If the URL is HTML and hasn't been scraped, queues it for scraping

# This requires:
# - A global cache: URL -> LinkResult
# - Locking around cache operations
# - When scraping a page, mark it as "being scraped" before fetching

# Let me redesign:
# - fetcher: manages global URL cache and fetching
# - crawler: orchestrates the crawl

# Here's the algorithm:
# 1. For root URL:
#    - Fetch it (with redirect tracking)
#    - Mark final URL as visited
#    - Parse HTML, extract links
#    - For each link:
#      a. Add to global "to check" queue
#    - Process root page links
# 
# 2. "to check" queue processing:
#    - For each URL in queue:
#      a. If already in cache, skip
#      b. Fetch it, add to cache
#      c. If HTML and not yet scraped, add to "to scrape" queue
#
# 3. "to scrape" queue:
#    - For each URL in queue:
#      a. Extract links from its HTML
#      b. Add new links to "to check" queue

# The key: separating "link checking" (get status) from "page scraping" (get links)
# A single fetch can do both

# Let me think about how the original might work:
# It probably has a "page" concept vs "link" concept
# - Pages are HTML pages that get scraped
# - Links are any URL that gets status-checked
# - An HTML page is also a link (gets status-checked) and also scraped

# The deduplication: "visited" set tracks URLs that have been or are being processed
# When a URL is first added to visited, it gets queued for processing
# When processing: fetch it once, get status + body (if HTML)

# OK so my approach should be:
# 1. Global "checked" map: URL -> LinkResult (stores status/error)
# 2. When checking a link: 
#    - If in checked map, return cached result
#    - Otherwise, fetch it and store in checked map
# 3. When scraping: use the body from the fetch (need to cache body too)

# This is getting complex. Let me think of a simpler approach that avoids double-fetching:

# Simpler approach:
# - When we decide to scrape a URL, we DO THE FETCH in the scrape goroutine
# - The link check result for that URL comes from the scrape fetch
# - But how does the parent page know the result?

# Actually the cleanest approach is:
# - Use a sync.Map (or mutex-protected map) for URL results
# - When processing any URL, first check if it's already been processed
# - If not: acquire a per-URL lock, fetch it, store result, release lock
# - Other goroutines waiting for the same URL get the cached result

# Let me implement this properly
echo "need to redesign crawler"

# for HTTPS external connections
# 
# The "dialing to the given TCP address timed out" is a fasthttp error for WHEN DIAL TIMES OUT
# vs "timeout" for when connection is established but response takes too long
# 
# In the original, the external HTTPS server times out at the TCP connection level (TCP SYN not answered)
# while in my case, the timeout is for the whole request
# 
# Actually, looking at the test again:
# The original shows "dialing to the given TCP address timed out" for https://example.com
# which is about TCP connection to port 443 timing out (the IP doesn't respond)
# 
# vs "timeout" for the slow server test on localhost (which accepts TCP but sends no response)
# 
# So the distinction:
# - "dialing to the given TCP address timed out" = TCP connection timed out (no response at TCP level)
# - "timeout" = HTTP request timed out after TCP connection established
# 
# In Go's net/http, both cases give "context deadline exceeded"
# But with different sub-errors:
# - TCP timeout: "context deadline exceeded" with no inner cause
# - HTTP timeout after connect: "context deadline exceeded (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)"
# 
# Wait, let me check what Go actually gives for a TCP connection timeout

# Actually, the distinction in the original fasthttp:
# - "dialing to the given TCP address timed out" = DialTimeout
# - "timeout" = ReadTimeout or WriteTimeout
# 
# In my implementation with Go's http.Client, Client.Timeout covers everything
# So I get the same error for both cases
# 
# The original binary uses fasthttp with separate dial and read timeouts
# 
# For the purpose of this implementation, "timeout" for all timeout errors should be acceptable
# But the HTTPS example.com case shows "dialing to the given TCP address timed out"

import (
    "context"

    "net"

    "strings"
    "time"
)

func formatNetError(err error) string {
    if err == nil {
        return ""
    }

# Great! Double-fetch is fixed! Each page is fetched only once
# Now the issue is the URL normalization in the link display
# 
# The HTML link "https://example.com" shows as "https://example.com/" in my output
# but original shows "https://example.com"
#
# I need to NOT normalize link URLs in the output
# The normalization should only happen for cache keys to prevent double-fetching
#
# Solution: separate "display URL" from "cache key URL"
# - When checking a link, use the normalized URL as cache key
# - But report the ORIGINAL URL in the result
#
# Wait, but if I have two different URLs that normalize to the same thing,
# they'd show as different URLs in the output but fetch the same resource
#
# Actually, the behavior I want is:
# 1. Links are displayed with the URL as-in-HTML (after resolving relative -> absolute)
# 2. But the deduplication and cache use normalized URLs
# 3. So "https://example.com" and "https://example.com/" would be treated as the same

# Let me think about this differently:
# - The "display URL" for a link is what the original shows in output
# - Let me check if the original normalizes "/" for page URLs in the output

# From test: 
# - http://localhost:8809 -> output shows "http://localhost:8809/"  (normalized)
# - https://example.com -> original shows "https://example.com" (NOT normalized)
# 
# Why does the root page show "/" but example.com doesn't?
# Because: when fetching http://localhost:8809, the server returns the page
# and the Response.Request.URL is "http://localhost:8809/" (or is it?)
#
# Wait, I tested this earlier:
# Final URL from Go's http.Client: "http://localhost:8813" (no slash!)
# But the original shows "http://localhost:8813/" (with slash)
# So the original normalizes the root page URL somehow
#
# Maybe the original uses the server's response URL + normalizes
# OR maybe it just adds "/" if path is empty

# My doFetch normalizes: "if pu.Path == "" { pu.Path = "/" }"
# So finalURL becomes "http://localhost:8813/"
# And that's used as the page URL - correct!

# For example.com, the HTML link is "https://example.com"
# In extractLinks, I have: "if resolved.Path == "" { resolved.Path = "/" }"
# This changes it to "https://example.com/" - WRONG for display

# So the fix: don't normalize in extractLinks
# But then the cache deduplication issue...

# Let me check: does the double-fetch issue only happen for ROOT pages?
# When a page's link is "http://some-server" (no slash), and we need to scrape it,
# we'd scrape "http://some-server" and the scrape would fetch it and get finalURL="http://some-server/"
# But is "http://some-server" already in scraped? YES (we marked it before scraping)
# And when scrapeURL returns, it marks finalURL="http://some-server/" as scraped too
# 
# The issue was: when /page links to "http://localhost:8813/", that's the LINK URL
# We'd try to queue scrape for "http://localhost:8813/"
# But our scraped set has "http://localhost:8813" (the original target URL) not "http://localhost:8813/"
# 
# MY FIX: In run(), I also mark "rootPageURL" (which is the normalized final URL) as scraped
# So now "http://localhost:8813/" IS in scraped
# And when /page links to "http://localhost:8813/", maybeQueueScrape checks scraped and finds it -> SKIP
# 
# But I removed normalization from extractLinks... will this still work?

# Let me test: with my current code (without normalization in extractLinks)
# 1. targetURL = "http://localhost:8813" (no slash) -> normalized to "http://localhost:8813/" by normalizeURL in run()
# 2. Actually wait, normalizeURL IS called in run() now! targetURL = normalizeURL(targetURL)
# 3. So targetURL becomes "http://localhost:8813/"
# 4. fetchAndCache("http://localhost:8813/") caches "http://localhost:8813/"
# 5. rootPageURL = "http://localhost:8813/" (from doFetch which normalizes)
# 6. Both are marked scraped
# 7. processPage extracts links from HTML
# 8. extractLinks resolves relative URLs against "http://localhost:8813/"
#    - "/" -> "http://localhost:8813/"
#    - "/page" -> "http://localhost:8813/page"
# 9. But the HTML in root page is <a href="/page"> which is resolved to "http://localhost:8813/page"
# 10. The HTML in /page is <a href="/"> which is resolved to "http://localhost:8813/"
# 11. When /page tries to queue "http://localhost:8813/", it's in scraped -> SKIP!
# 
# So actually, with normalizeURL in run() for the targetURL,
# and with the finalURL normalization in doFetch,
# I DON'T need normalization in extractLinks for this specific case!
#
# Let me remove the normalization from extractLinks and check behavior

sed -i 's/\t\t\/\/ Normalize: ensure path is not empty\n\t\tif resolved.Path == "" {//' /workspace/muffet/html.go
cat /workspace/muffet/html.go | grep -A3 "ensure path"

# External HTTPS still shows "timeout" instead of "error when dialing IP: dialing to the given TCP address timed out"
# Because in this environment, the HTTPS connection to example.com is timing out at the HTTP level
# (context deadline exceeded), not at the TCP dial level (i.o timeout)
# 
# This is because example.com is NOT firewalled here - it's just slow (or accepting connections but not responding)
# Actually wait - it could be that the IP is reachable at TCP level but then TLS handshake times out
# Or the server accepts TCP but is slow to respond to HTTP
# 
# In the original binary, the error "dialing to the given TCP address timed out" suggests
# the TCP connection itself is timing out (the IP doesn't respond to SYN packets)
# 
# But when I use a DialTimeout in Go, the dial uses a separate timeout and if the dial succeeds
# but the HTTP request is slow, we get "context deadline exceeded"
#
# The behavior depends on the network. If example.com is firewalled (SYN dropped), we get i/o timeout
# If it accepts TCP but is slow, we get context deadline exceeded
# 
# Looking at the test environment: the original binary gets "dialing to the given TCP address timed out"
# which means the TCP connection to example.com is being silently dropped (firewall)
# In my test, I'm getting "context deadline exceeded" which means TCP connects but HTTP times out
# 
# This is a network environment difference. Let me check:

cat > /tmp/test_tcp.go << 'EOF'
package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "net"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    // Try to TCP connect to example.com:443
    d := net.Dialer{Timeout: 3 * time.Second}
    ctx := context.Background()
    start := time.Now()
    conn, err := d.DialContext(ctx, "tcp", "172.66.147.243:443")
    elapsed := time.Since(start)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Printf("Error after %v: %v\n", elapsed, err)
    } else {
        conn.Close()
        fmt.Printf("Connected after %v\n", elapsed)
    }
}
EOF
timeout 5 go run /tmp/test_tcp.go 2>&1

# Because in this environment, the HTTPS connection to example.com is timing out at the HTTP level
# (context deadline exceeded), not at the TCP dial level (i.o timeout)
# 
# This is because example.com is NOT firewalled here - it's just slow (or accepting connections but not responding)
# Actually wait - it could be that the IP is reachable at TCP level but then TLS handshake times out
# Or the server accepts TCP but is slow to respond to HTTP
# 
# In the original binary, the error "dialing to the given TCP address timed out" suggests
# the TCP connection itself is timing out (the IP doesn't respond to SYN packets)
# 
# But when I use a DialTimeout in Go, the dial uses a separate timeout and if the dial succeeds
# but the HTTP request is slow, we get "context deadline exceeded"
#
# The behavior depends on the network. If example.com is firewalled (SYN dropped), we get i/o timeout
# If it accepts TCP but is slow, we get context deadline exceeded
# 
# Looking at the test environment: the original binary gets "dialing to the given TCP address timed out"
# which means the TCP connection to example.com is being silently dropped (firewall)
# In my test, I'm getting "context deadline exceeded" which means TCP connects but HTTP times out
# 
# This is a network environment difference. Let me check:

cat > /tmp/test_tcp.go << 'EOF'
package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "net"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    // Try to TCP connect to example.com:443
    d := net.Dialer{Timeout: 3 * time.Second}
    ctx := context.Background()
    start := time.Now()
    conn, err := d.DialContext(ctx, "tcp", "172.66.147.243:443")
    elapsed := time.Since(start)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Printf("Error after %v: %v\n", elapsed, err)
    } else {
        conn.Close()
        fmt.Printf("Connected after %v\n", elapsed)
    }
}
EOF

# My implementation doesn't handle this case!
#

# - fr.body will be nil (because isHTML is false)

# - Result: empty output with exit 0
# 
# I need to check: if the root page is not HTML, it's a fatal error
# Let me fix this

cat > /tmp/fix_nonhtml.py << 'EOF'
with open('/workspace/muffet/main.go', 'r') as f:
    content = f.read()

old = '''	// Fetch root page
	fr := c.fetchAndCache(targetURL)
	if fr.errMsg != "" {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to fetch root page: %s", fr.errMsg)
	}'''

new = '''	// Fetch root page
	fr := c.fetchAndCache(targetURL)
	if fr.errMsg != "" {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to fetch root page: %s", fr.errMsg)
	}
	if fr.body == nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to fetch root page: root page has invalid content type")
	}'''

content = content.replace(old, new)

with open('/workspace/muffet/main.go', 'w') as f:
    f.write(content)
print("Done")
EOF

# Restart all test servers

# Kill all background Python processes

sleep 1

python3 /tmp/test_server2.py &  # port 8766  
python3 /tmp/test_server3.py &  # port 8767
sleep 2

echo "=== Final comprehensive tests ==="

# Run the same tests as before

    "http://localhost:8765 -e example.com"
    "http://localhost:8765 -v -e example.com"
    "http://localhost:8766"

    "http://localhost:8767 -v"

    "http://localhost:8765 -i localhost"
    "--version"
    "--help"
    ""
)

        echo "  MINE: $mine"
        echo "  ORIG: $orig"
        fail=$((fail+1))
    fi
done

echo ""
echo "Results: $pass passed, $fail failed"
